record.summary: The Charlotte City Council unanimously approved a 150-day moratorium on new data centers on June 8, 2026, described in coverage as the largest US city to pause data-center development, running through November 5, 2026. Already-approved projects are exempt. A city staff study submitted September 1, 2026 found data-center impacts vary widely by facility type, site layout and climate; the Transportation, Planning and Development Committee then recommended the full council extend the pause by up to nine months (WSOC/WFAE) to allow more time on air-pollution monitoring, noise limits and community input. GovTech (Sept. 29, 2026) reports the council set a public hearing for October 12 so residents get a final say before the council's vote, and describes the proposed extension as 11 months, through October 11, 2027, which differs from the nine months reported earlier; the sources conflict on length. As of October 18, 2026 no source checked reports the outcome of the hearing or a final council vote on the extension; the moratorium as enacted remains in effect through November 5, 2026 either way. Status: enacted (original 150-day pause).

record.next_milestone: Oct. 6, 2026: Duke Energy North Carolina, Amazon Data Services, Andale LLC, Carolina Industrial Group for Fair Utility Rates II and III, the U.S. Department of Defense and other federal executive agencies, Google LLC and Microsoft Corporation filed an Agreement and Stipulation of Settlement on Large Load Tariff in Docket Nos. E-7 Sub 1329 and E-2 Sub 1380. Per the filing, the tariff applies to total contract demand of 50 MW or more with an expected 80% or higher load factor, or 150 MW or more at any load factor, bills demand charges at no less than 75% of contract demand, and would take effect for service on and after January 1, 2027 if the Commission approves it. The settlement sets no hearing or decision date, and the Commission may 'investigate, accept, or reject the terms contained in this Stipulation, in whole, or in part.' No NCUC order had been announced as of October 18, 2026. Earlier: a Second Amended Comprehensive Revenue Requirement Agreement and Stipulation of Settlement (Duke Energy Carolinas, NCUC Public Staff, industrial/customer groups, Microsoft; Andale later added) was filed July 17, 2026 and amended July 20; on September 14, 2026 Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who declined to sign it, filed a proposal for a new rate class for data centers and other large-load customers; and on September 18, 2026 the NCUC voted to deny Duke Energy Progress a certificate for a gas turbine at the Smith Energy Complex, finding Duke had not adequately shown how it complies with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge (WUNC).
record.summary: Duke Energy's proposed 2026 rate-case settlement commits it to an expedited proceeding to establish a formal Large Load Tariff before new rates take effect. Governor Josh Stein and Attorney General Jeff Jackson are pressing Duke — a Ratepayer Protection Pledge signatory — to make the federal pledge binding: "Now, Duke Energy must make that voluntary pledge real. The North Carolina Utilities Commission and Duke Energy must create a legally binding large-load tariff to charge data centers their full freight" (Stein). Duke's spokesperson responds that "data centers and other large-load customers must pay the costs required to serve them while creating long-term value for existing customers." On October 6, 2026 Duke and several data-center operators filed a separate settlement on the large-load tariff itself; it requires NCUC approval before it takes effect.

record.notes: 1 GW hyperscale campus on a 282-acre site in Wayne County (north of I-94, between Haggerty Road and I-275), originally advanced as 'Project Cannoli'. Power served by 2.7 GW of new DTE solar, storage and demand response. Service start targeted December 2027, full capacity December 2028. Google announced a $10M Energy Impact Fund for Michigan energy affordability. The project went through a contested case before the Michigan Public Service Commission (docket U-22058); as of early Sept 2026 the Attorney General was still pressing for a 90% minimum billing demand (vs. DTE's proposed 80%) and stronger exit-fee terms. On Oct 1, 2026 the Commission voted unanimously to grant conditional approval of DTE's special contracts for the project; per Michigan Public, the contracts must cover generation, transmission, distribution and other costs, with a minimum monthly billing demand of 80% of the contract capacity and a termination payment ensuring Google LLC pays at least 15 years of minimum monthly charges. Local opposition includes a 1,500+ signature petition. May 19, 2026: Van Buren Township's Board of Trustees unanimously approved a 50% property tax exemption for 15 years for the project, with a Real Industrial Facilities Tax Exemption for a 36-month construction period; Google is to pay the township $15.4 million for township-wide capital projects. Oct 1, 2026: the Wayne County Commission overrode County Executive Warren Evans' Sept 25 veto of the project's tax incentives by a 13-0 vote (Fox 2 Detroit); the same day the Michigan Public Service Commission voted unanimously to grant conditional approval of DTE's power contracts for the project (Planet Detroit). Oct 14, 2026: the Van Buren Township Planning Commission approved the final site plan 5-1; Panattoni entered into an operational agreement with the township on issues outside the commission's scope.

record.notes: Proposed AWS campus on ~2,050 acres (a 965-acre northern parcel and a 1,085-acre southern parcel) adjacent to Constellation Energy's Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant at 1650 Calvert Cliffs Parkway, Lusby. The concept calls for up to eight data center buildings (266,000-332,000 sq ft each) across three campuses, ~2.46M sq ft total. AWS publicly introduced the project at a Calvert County community meeting on March 31, 2026 and filed a concept site plan application on May 4, 2026; no construction permits have been issued. Air-cooled design (cited as ~96% of the year); reported at ~1.5 GW, a figure AWS has not officially disclosed. The proposal drew local opposition, and county commissioners attempted an unsuccessful temporary moratorium on data center development. On August 4, 2026 Calvert County announced that AWS had formally withdrawn its plans for the campus; Constellation, which owns the plant, said AWS has withdrawn its plans and that it continues to work with the county and state (WTOP). record.notes: Microsoft's first Wisconsin data center, branded 'Fairwater.' On June 23, 2026 Microsoft announced the first Fairwater facility is fully operational (equipment brought online in April 2026), with roughly 550 on-site full-time employees — expected to reach about 800 once the second facility opens — and about $4.7 billion in projected 2024–2028 Wisconsin hyperscale construction spending, including direct purchases from 29 Wisconsin businesses across 11 counties.
